1.slug: EXT. ROME — A STREET NEAR THE FORUM — DAY
1.voice: Outdoors on a crowded, noisy holiday street: a raised, projected voice that carries over the crowd
open: February, 44 BC. The Feast of Lupercal. Garlands hang from the statues; the shops are shuttered for the holiday.
A THRONG OF CITIZENS pours down the street toward the Forum — tradesmen in their best tunics, laughing, shoving, a few waving sprigs of laurel for Caesar.
Laughter, shouting, whistling — a holiday crowd in full cry.

Hooves on the stones. Two TRIBUNES ride into the crowd and rein in hard: FLAVIUS, hard and quick, and MARULLUS, older, colder. The horses snort and stamp, pacing back and forth. The purple stripe on their togas stops the crowd dead.

5: A broad-shouldered CARPENTER is shoved to the front by the men behind him.
7: Beside him, a wiry COBBLER with a grin that has never once been respectful. He plays to the crowd behind him.
13: The crowd laughs. Marullus does not.
18: Marullus mounts the base of a statue so the whole street can see him.
19: The crowd has gone quiet, shamed. Caps come off.
21: The crowd melts away; the shuffling and the noise die to nothing. Flavius and Marullus are left alone among the garlands.
23: Flavius reaches up and tears a wreath from a statue of Caesar. He drops it in the dust, wheels his horse and rides down the street, overturning the stalls; his shouts carry back over Marullus.

paren.4: from the saddle — angry, scolding, condescending; the questions sharp and badgering
paren.18: sharp, exasperated — let each question hang

2.slug: EXT. ROME — THE VIA SACRA, A PUBLIC PLACE — DAY
2.voice: Outdoors in a public street during a procession, music and crowds nearby: a projected voice; quieter and closer when two speak apart
open: Flutes and drums. The PROCESSION fills the street: lictors with their rods, then CAESAR in a purple toga and a laurel wreath, borne along on the roar of the crowd.

Beside him CALPURNIA, his wife, veiled. MARK ANTONY, stripped to a goatskin for the sacred race, bouncing on his toes. Behind them the great men of Rome: DECIUS, CICERO, CASCA — and, a little apart from the rest, BRUTUS and CASSIUS.
Somewhere in the press, an old SOOTHSAYER pushes forward.

3: Caesar raises a hand. The procession halts.
8: Calpurnia steps to the edge of the course. Antony grins at her.
14: A thin cry cuts through the music. Heads turn.
18: The crowd parts. The SOOTHSAYER stands alone in the open street — blind, ragged, utterly still.
23: Cassius takes the old man by the arm and leads him to Caesar. Caesar studies his face for a long moment.
26: Caesar laughs it off. The procession moves on.
28: The street empties around BRUTUS and CASSIUS. Far off, the roar of the games.
32: Cassius moves closer. They walk together, slowly, under the colonnade.
40: Brutus stops dead, looking toward the noise.
46: Cassius drops his voice. Brutus does not look at him.
50: The procession returns. Caesar walks fast, his face set. Calpurnia pale. The others follow in an uneasy silence.
54: Caesar stops — and looks straight at Cassius across the street. Then he beckons Antony close.
60: CASCA lingers, then ambles over, brushing at the sleeve Brutus pulled.
76: Casca mimes it — the fall, the foaming mouth — enjoying himself.
95: Casca saunters off, whistling. Brutus watches him go.
100: Cassius alone. The cheerful mask drops from his face.

3.voice: Outdoors at night in a violent thunderstorm: voices raised over wind, rain and thunder
open: The night before the Ides of March. A storm the city will talk about for a hundred years.

Lightning splits the sky. Rain sheets across the paving. CASCA comes running down the empty street, sword drawn, soaked and wild-eyed — and almost collides with CICERO, wrapped in his cloak, walking home as if nothing were the matter.

6: Thunder. Casca grips Cicero’s arm; his words tumble out.
11: Cicero pulls his cloak tight and goes. Casca is alone in the storm.
12: A figure strides out of the rain: CASSIUS, bareheaded, his cloak open to the lightning.
19: Cassius throws his arms wide to the storm.
25: Cassius draws a dagger and holds it up in the lightning.
31: Footsteps. Both men shrink back into a doorway. CINNA hurries past — then stops, peering at them.
39: Cassius pulls out a packet of papers, sealed, and presses them into Cinna’s hands.
43: Cinna runs off into the rain. Cassius turns to Casca with a fierce smile.
